highlighted_obligation.description: Postcondition P4: Creates PAYOUT transaction when payout > 0 and no duplicate exists.
highlighted_obligation.plain_description: When money is due and no payment exists yet, exactly one payment record must be created.

obligation_read_model.claim_ceiling: An Obligation is an engine-derived testing artifact, not a DomainSpec meta-type. Derivable-pure does not mean a test passed.

formal_clause.plain_precondition: The player has money to receive, and we have not paid it before.
formal_clause.plain_postcondition: Create one payment record and one confirmation that it happened.
formal_clause.claim_ceiling: P4 is a candidate clause in the minted read model.

proof_plan.plain_question: When money is due and no payout exists, does the system create one payout record and then announce one PayoutCreated event — without doing either twice?

observations.label: The record is written before the event

proof_plan.claim_ceiling: The pure R5 decision has generated checks. The full FS-POST-001 postcondition is skipped, and the existing handwritten checks are not machine-bound to that obligation.

code_contract.decision: allow only a positive first payout
effects: emit one PayoutCreated event after the write
code_contract.claim_ceiling: This describes the required software shape. It does not generate an implementation.

code_realization.plain_summary: The existing code first decides whether a payout is allowed, writes the payout, and only then emits PayoutCreated when an event handler is present.
code_realization.claim_ceiling: This is a shortened explanation of existing handwritten TypeScript. The optional event handler means the current code does not unconditionally guarantee P4 as written.

negative_control.setup: Allow a positive first payout but provide no event handler.
negative_control.expected_observation: The payout record can be written while PayoutCreated is absent.

verification.completion_rule: Issue a proof receipt only after one obligation-bound harness observes the write, the event, their order, duplicate suppression, and the negative control.

steps.title: A player should be paid once — never twice
steps.plain_language: We begin with the promise people care about. No diagrams, files, or technical names are needed yet.

steps.title: DomainSpec names the business ideas
steps.plain_language: The promise points to four business ideas. DomainSpec gives each one a stable identity and type, then we highlight the Operation: what the business does when the promise applies.

steps.title: DomainSpec makes the promise precise
steps.plain_language: The DomainSpec semantic graph records when the promise applies, what must happen, and in which order. That removes guesswork while keeping the business meaning.

steps.title: DomainSpec derives something to check
steps.plain_language: The test-derivation model emits an Obligation: a promise the finished system must be able to prove. It is a derived checking artifact, not a DomainSpec meta-type and not proof that the system already works.

steps.title: See the other promises that must hold
steps.plain_language: This payment promise is one of 79 checks for the feature. Some are simple, some need the running system, and one still needs deeper formal work.

steps.title: Keep DomainSpec's three models separate
steps.plain_language: The authored feature explains the business, the DomainSpec semantic graph removes ambiguity, and test derivation lists what must be proven. They work together, but none can replace the others.

steps.title: Follow DomainSpec toward proof and code
steps.plain_language: The ontology now shows the DomainSpec semantic graph, DS-D1 Operation type, derived Obligation, candidate architecture type, proof gaps, and existing code as separate connected nodes.

steps.title: Map the DomainSpec Operation to a code shape
steps.plain_language: Now we decide how the business action may appear in software: what enters, what decision is made, and which effects must happen in order.

steps.title: See how that contract appears in real code
steps.plain_language: The current TypeScript makes the payout decision, writes the payment, and then emits the event. It was written by people; the ontology did not generate it.

steps.title: Run the proof against the code
steps.plain_language: We bring the proof plan and the implementation together. Existing checks cover important pieces, but one bound check must still observe the complete promise and a deliberate failure.

steps.title: Call it proven only when the evidence is complete
steps.plain_language: Today the honest verdict is partial: the code and several checks exist, but FS-POST-001 is still skipped and no receipt binds the whole result to the obligation.

proof_boundary: This guide shows how a business promise becomes a model, a proof plan, a code contract, and executable evidence. For FS-POST-001 the current evidence is partial: code and separate checks exist, but the full obligation remains skipped and unbound.
